00 / BEFORE YOU PRESS PLAY

Read the model. Set the problem. Take one step.

Already familiar? Go to the experiment ↓

A numerical solution needs three ingredients: an equation that describes change, an initial profile, and rules for the ends of the domain. The computer then advances cell averages through small time steps.

1 / What does Burgers’ equation describe?

Think of u(x,t) as a velocity-like scalar along a one-dimensional line. Unlike linear convection with a prescribed speed, the local wave speed here is u itself. Positive values travel right; negative values travel left. Burgers’ equation is an idealized model of nonlinear transport and viscous smoothing, rather than a complete model of compressible gas flow.

First · non-conservative form
∂u/∂t + u ∂u/∂x = ν ∂²u/∂x²

For a smooth inviscid solution, this makes the local characteristic speed u explicit.

Then · conservative form
∂u/∂t + ∂f(u)/∂x = ν ∂²u/∂x²,   f(u) = u²/2

This flux form underlies the finite-volume balance used by all four methods.

∂u/∂tLocal change

How the value changes at a fixed location.

+
∂(u²/2)/∂xNonlinear transport

A spatial difference in flux moves the conserved quantity between neighbors.

=
ν ∂²u/∂x²Physical diffusion

Viscosity ν ≥ 0 smooths gradients. ν = 0 is the inviscid equation.

The two forms are equivalent for differentiable solutions because ∂(u²/2)/∂x = u ∂u/∂x. When ν = 0 and a shock forms, the classical product u ∂u/∂x is not defined at the jump; the conservative weak formulation supplies the correct jump balance, together with the entropy condition. Set ν = 0 in either displayed equation for the inviscid model. Here x ∈ [0,1] and the numerical parameters are nondimensional; in dimensional variables, u has units of length/time and ν has units of length²/time.

2 / Initial condition: what is there at t = 0?

An initial condition specifies u(x,0) = u₀(x) everywhere. Start with a smooth profile to watch a shock emerge, or a two-state jump to study a Riemann problem.

This figure follows the problem selected in the experiment below. Dashed reference curves in the method plots show the exact solution, not another numerical scheme.

3 / Boundary conditions: what happens at the ends?

The interior update needs neighbors outside the domain. Ghost cells provide those values; they are bookkeeping cells outside the N physical cells.

SMOOTH PROFILES · PERIODIC DOMAIN

u(x+1,t) = u(x,t). The left ghost copies the last cell; the right ghost copies the first. x = 0 and x = 1 are the same periodic location. The smooth pulse is periodic too, so it has no hidden seam jump. The diagram shows one ghost layer; MUSCL also reads a second layer for reconstruction.

At each stage time, this lab fills exterior cell averages from the known whole-line shock, fan, or viscous traveling wave. These are controlled reference boundaries, not solid walls or a generic outflow condition.

Periodic runs conserve ΣūᵢΔx. In open-domain cases it can change through the boundary fluxes; the conservation residual in each card accounts for that change.

Choose an initial condition below ↓

4 / How does the computer solve it?

Split [0,1] into N cells of width Δx = 1/N. Store the cell average ūᵢ, not a continuously varying curve. A numerical flux Fᵢ₊½ estimates transport through the face between two cells.

ūᵢⁿ⁺¹ = ūᵢⁿ + (Δt/Δx)(Fᵢ₋½ − Fᵢ₊½)

New amount = old amount + incoming − outgoing. Here n labels time and i labels a cell. If more leaves than enters, the average decreases. The same face flux enters one cell and leaves its neighbor, so interior transfers cancel in the total balance. Face arrows define the positive-x sign convention; the balance uses signed total fluxes.

GODUNOV

Solve a local wave problem.

constant cells → Riemann flux → one update

Use the entropy solution between two neighboring states to choose the face flux. Robust at shocks; first-order numerical diffusion broadens fronts.

RUSANOV

Average the flux, add damping.

left / right states → damped flux → one update

Average the two physical fluxes and subtract a jump term scaled by the fastest local speed. This helps control oscillations but can smear a front.

MUSCL + SSP-RK2

Reconstruct, then take two stages.

limited slopes → Godunov flux → stage 1 → stage 2

Reconstruct a line in each cell with the MC limiter, then use two time stages. Higher smooth accuracy; the limiter reduces slopes near troublesome gradients.

MACCORMACK

Predict, then correct.

forward predictor → backward corrector → average

Evaluate flux differences in opposite directions in the two stages. Accurate for smooth waves, but using these differences without a limiter can create wiggles near shocks.

5 / Read the output as evidence.

Profile: compare numerical cell averages with the exact curve. Signed error: see whether the method is above or below the exact cell average. L₁ / RMS: compare error magnitudes at the same physical time. A small conservation residual checks the balance, not the accuracy of the shape.

Predict before you run.

Which side moves faster? Will it compress or spread? For smooth inviscid data, predict tₛ = −1/min u₀′. Use a small enough Δt to resolve both transport and diffusion; the default factor is 0.45. A stable run may still be smeared or oscillatory.

After smooth-wave breaking, the classical exact reference stops; the numerical solution continues. Do not interpret the omitted error as zero.

02 / UNDERSTAND THE WAVES

Fast catches slow. Slow falls behind.

Your characteristic diagram

Error across time

L₁ = Σ|ūᵢ − ūᵢ,exact| Δx. Colors match the method cards. Zero errors are omitted from the log plot. For smooth periodic profiles, the classical reference stops at the predicted tₛ; the numerical solutions continue beyond shock formation.

a / SHOCK

Characteristics collide.

For uL > uR, compression forms an entropy shock. Conservation fixes its speed:

s = [f]/[u] = (uL + uR)/2

A method can look smooth and stable yet move a shock incorrectly. Conservative flux differences preserve the correct jump balance.

b / RAREFACTION

Characteristics spread.

For uL < uR, the entropy solution is a fan. Inside it:

u(x,t) = (x − x₀)/t

The transonic case crosses u = 0. A stationary expansion jump is a weak solution but violates the entropy condition. Godunov selects the fan.

c / VISCOSITY

A shock gains a thickness.

For ν > 0, physical diffusion competes with steepening. A traveling-wave reference is:

u = s − (Δu/2) tanh[Δu(x−x₀−st)/(4ν)]

Its characteristic thickness is 4ν/Δu. Compare it with Δx: a stable time step cannot compensate for an unresolved transition.

03 / NUMERICAL ALGORITHMS

From one cell to the next.

ūᵢⁿ⁺¹ = ūᵢⁿ − (Δt/Δx)(Fᵢ₊½ − Fᵢ₋½)

f(u) = u²/2. The total interface flux includes diffusion: F = Fadv − ν(ūi+1−ūi)/Δx.

1 / Fill ghost cells

Periodic copies for smooth profiles. Otherwise, exact whole-line cell averages at the current stage time.

2 / Build interface states

Piecewise constants, or MC-limited linear reconstruction for MUSCL.

3 / Evaluate the flux

One shared interface flux enters neighboring cells with opposite signs.

4 / Advance the time level

Forward Euler, SSP-RK2, or MacCormack’s predictor–corrector. Refill ghosts at each stage.

MethodInterface / time algorithmWhat to inspectTime-step guidance
GodunovExact scalar Riemann flux; forward EulerEntropy selection; first-order smearingC + 2D ≤ 1 for the first-order monotone update
Rusanov½(fL+fR) − ½a(ūR−ūL); a = max(|ūL|,|ūR|)Robustness; numerical diffusionC + 2D ≤ 1 is the standard monotone-step bound
MUSCL · SSP-RK2MC-limited slopes, Godunov flux; two-stage SSP-RK2Sharper fronts; reduced order near extrema/jumpsUse C + 2D ≤ 0.5 as a conservative working guideline
MacCormackForward flux predictor; backward flux corrector; centered viscosity in both stagesSecond-order smooth accuracy; oscillations near shocksC ≤ 1 for linearized inviscid constant-state analysis; no nonlinear monotonicity guarantee

C = max|u| Δt/Δx, D = νΔt/Δx². These explicit schemes have a diffusion restriction as well as an advective CFL restriction. The cards show C + 2D for the actual last step, using the maximum speed over both stages when applicable. A bound on a local linearization does not establish nonlinear stability or entropy convergence. Default factor 0.45 is intended for all four methods.

Open the flux formulas and two-stage algorithms
Godunov: if uL ≤ uR, use f(uL) for uL ≥ 0, f(uR) for uR ≤ 0, otherwise 0.
If uL > uR, use f(uL) when uL + uR ≥ 0, otherwise f(uR).
MUSCL: σᵢ = minmod(2δ₋uᵢ, (δ₋uᵢ + δ₊uᵢ)/2, 2δ₊uᵢ)
       uLᵢ₊½ = ūᵢ + σᵢ/2; uRᵢ₊½ = ūᵢ₊₁ − σᵢ₊₁/2
SSP-RK2: u* = uⁿ + Δt L(uⁿ,tⁿ)
         uⁿ⁺¹ = ½uⁿ + ½[u* + Δt L(u*,tⁿ+Δt)]
MacCormack: u*ᵢ = uⁿᵢ − λ[f(uⁿᵢ₊₁)−f(uⁿᵢ)] + Dδ²uⁿᵢ
           uⁿ⁺¹ᵢ = ½{uⁿᵢ + u*ᵢ − λ[f(u*ᵢ)−f(u*ᵢ₋₁)] + Dδ²u*ᵢ}

λ = Δt/Δx. The viscous term uses cell-centered differences, independent of the limited advective reconstruction. Smooth-order statements assume resolved, smooth solutions; errors near shocks generally converge more slowly.

04 / LAB WORKSHEET

Predict. Run. Explain.

Use the same final time when comparing meshes or methods. Export the arrays to support your conclusions.

  1. Shock speed. Predict s for 1 → 0. At t = 0.4, where should a shock starting at x₀ = 0.3 be? Compare all four profiles.
  2. Entropy matters. Run −1 → 1. Explain why the entropy solution is a spreading fan rather than a stationary discontinuity.
  3. Refine the mesh. Compare N = 80, 160, 320 at fixed factor and time. Compute p = ln(EN/E2N)/ln 2 using L₁ error. Repeat with the viscous shock.
  4. Separate physical and numerical diffusion. Reduce ν from 0.02 to 0.005. Is 4ν/Δu resolved by your mesh? Which method smears the layer most?
  5. Cross the time-step limit. Use “Cross the CFL limit”. Record C + 2D, min/max values and error. Explain why bounded oscillations differ from growing instability.
  6. Watch a smooth wave break. Compare the sine, two-wave sine and smooth periodic pulse. Change A and predict tₛ = −1/min(u₀′). At A = ½, a single sine has tₛ = 1/π. Explain why the classical exact curve disappears at that time.
